sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Jesus was the greatest teacher who ever lived, and one of His favorite ways to teach was by telling stories. These stories are called parables. A parable is a simple story taken from everyday life — farming, sheep, families, travelers — that carries a deeper truth about God and His kingdom. In fact, Matthew tells us that Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables, and without a parable He did not speak to them.

Today we'll look at four of His best-loved parables: the Sower, the Good Samaritan, the Lost Sheep, and the Prodigal Son. As you listen, try to picture yourself in each story. Which character are you most like?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
Let's begin with the Parable of the Sower, from Matthew chapter thirteen. Jesus said that a farmer went out to sow seed. As he scattered it by hand, some seed fell by the wayside, on the hard path, and the birds came and ate it up. Some fell on stony places, where there wasn't much soil. It sprang up quickly, but when the sun came up, it was scorched, and because it had no root, it withered away. Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it. But other seed fell into good ground and brought forth fruit — some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.

Jesus explained the story to His disciples. In Luke's Gospel He says plainly: “The seed is the word of God.” The hard path is like a person who hears God's word but doesn't understand it, and the wicked one snatches it away. The stony ground is like a person who receives the word with joy, but when trouble comes, gives up. The thorny ground is like a person whose faith is choked by the cares of this world and the love of riches. And the good ground? Matthew chapter thirteen, verse twenty-three: “But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit.”

Next is the Parable of the Good Samaritan, from Luke chapter ten. A lawyer asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus asked what the law said, and the man answered: love God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus said, you have answered right. But the man, wanting to justify himself, asked, “And who is my neighbour?”

Jesus answered with a story. A man was traveling from Jerusalem down to Jericho, and he fell among thieves, who stripped him, wounded him, and left him half dead. A priest came by, saw him, and passed by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, did the same. Then a Samaritan came along. In those days, Jews and Samaritans would have nothing to do with each other. But when the Samaritan saw the wounded man, he had compassion on him. He bandaged his wounds, poured in oil and wine, set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. The next day he paid the innkeeper and said, take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you.

Jesus asked, which of these three was a neighbor to the man who fell among thieves? The lawyer said, “He that shewed mercy on him.” And Jesus said, “Go, and do thou likewise.”

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
In Luke chapter fifteen, the religious leaders were complaining that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them. So Jesus told three stories about lost things being found.

The first is the Parable of the Lost Sheep. Luke chapter fifteen, verse four: “What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?” When the shepherd finds it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and calls his friends and neighbors to celebrate. Jesus said there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

Then Jesus told the Parable of the Prodigal Son. A man had two sons. The younger son said, father, give me my share of the inheritance now. In that culture, asking for it while the father was still alive was a deep insult. But the father divided his property between them. The younger son went to a far country and wasted everything on wild living. Then a famine came, and he was so desperate that he took a job feeding pigs, and he would gladly have eaten the pigs' food, but no one gave him anything.

Finally he came to himself. He thought, my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, and here I am starving. I will go to my father and say, I have sinned, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me one of your hired servants.

Luke chapter fifteen, verse twenty: “And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” The son began his speech, but the father interrupted. He called for the best robe, a ring for his hand, shoes for his feet, and the fatted calf for a feast. “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”

But the older brother, coming in from the field, was angry and refused to join the party. I've served you all these years, he said, and you never threw a feast for me. The father went out and pleaded with him too: son, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours. It was right to celebrate, because your brother was lost, and is found.

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What do these parables teach us?

The Parable of the Sower asks: what kind of soil is my heart? God's word is powerful, but we must receive it, hold on to it through hard times, and not let worries and possessions choke it out.

The Good Samaritan teaches that a neighbor is anyone in need — even someone different from us, even someone we've been taught to avoid. Love is not just a feeling; it is stopping, helping, and paying the cost.

The Lost Sheep shows us that every single person matters to God. If you've ever felt like just one in a crowd, remember: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find the one.

And the Prodigal Son shows us the heart of our Father in heaven. No matter how far we've wandered, He is watching the road, ready to run to us when we turn back. And it also warns us not to be like the older brother, who was close to the father in body but far from him in heart.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Which character did you see yourself in today? The wandering son? The older brother? The wounded traveler? The one who passed by? Talk to God honestly about it.

Let's pray. Father, thank You that You search for the lost and run to welcome us home. Make my heart good soil for Your word. Open my eyes to the people around me who need mercy, and help me go and do likewise. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll look at the most important events in history: the death and resurrection of Jesus.
